claim: Rett Syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder resulting from mutations in the gene MECP2.
source: Rett Syndrome is a devastating neurodevelopmental disorder resulting from mutations in the gene MECP2.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as established background information about Rett Syndrome.

claim: Mutations of Mecp2 restricted to GABAergic cell types largely replicate the behavioral phenotypes associated with mouse models of Rett Syndrome.
source: Mutations of Mecp2 that are restricted to GABAergic cell types largely replicate the behavioral phenotypes associated with mouse models of Rett Syndrome, suggesting a pathophysiological role for inhibitory interneurons.
evidence: This statement references prior research findings about GABAergic-specific mutations.

claim: VIP interneurons may play a critical role in the proper development and function of cortical circuits.
source: Recent work has suggested that vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing (VIP) interneurons may play a critical role in the proper development and function of cortical circuits, making them a potential key point of vulnerability in neurodevelopmental disorders.
evidence: This statement references recent work suggesting a role for VIP interneurons.

claim: Loss of MeCP2 specifically from VIP interneurons replicates key neural and behavioral phenotypes observed following global Mecp2 loss of function.
source: Here we find that loss of MeCP2 specifically from VIP interneurons replicates key neural and behavioral phenotypes observed following global Mecp2 loss of function.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study as stated in the abstract.

claim: Nearly all PV interneurons expressed MeCP2.
source: As reported previously (Ito-Ishida et al., 2015), nearly all PV and SST interneurons expressed MeCP2.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data and references prior work.

claim: Nearly all SST interneurons expressed MeCP2.
source: As reported previously (Ito-Ishida et al., 2015), nearly all PV and SST interneurons expressed MeCP2.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data and references prior work.

claim: Approximately 80% of VIP interneurons expressed MeCP2.
source: In addition, ~80% of VIP interneurons expressed MeCP2, suggesting a previously unappreciated potential role for this signaling pathway in VIP interneuron development and function.
evidence: This is quantified from immunohistochemistry data presented in the study.

claim: Conditional mutants achieved near-complete removal of MeCP2 expression in each of the targeted interneuron classes.
source: We first examined the efficacy of conditional removal of MeCP2 from targeted interneuron populations in the cortex of Cre+Mecp2f/y animals, finding near-complete removal of MeCP2 expression in each of the targeted interneuron classes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The mean age of death in Mecp2–/y mutants was 71.5 ± 8.7 days.
source: We found that the mean age of death in Mecp2–/y (71.5 ± 8.7 days; n = 13; p<0.00001; H = 57.06)
evidence: This is a direct measurement from survival analysis.

claim: The mean age of death in Dlx5/6 mutants was 118.5 ± 15.2 days.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from survival analysis.

claim: The mean age of death in SST mutants was 172.5 ± 12.2 days.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from survival analysis.

claim: The mean age of death in PV mutants was 493.5 ± 6.5 days.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from survival analysis.

claim: The mean age of death in VIP mutants was 447.5 ± 52.5 days.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from survival analysis.

claim: The mean age of death in Mecp2–/y, Dlx5/6, and SST mutants was significantly decreased compared to Mecp2f/y controls.
source: We found that the mean age of death in Mecp2–/y (71.5 ± 8.7 days; n = 13; p<0.00001; H = 57.06), Dlx5/6 mutants (118.5 ± 15.2 days; n = 10; p<0.00001; H = 45.63), and SST mutants (172.5 ± 12.2 days; n = 16; p<0.0001; H = 36.30), but not PV (493.5 ± 6.5 days; n = 18; p>0.99; H = −3.50) or VIP mutants (447.5 ± 52.5 days; n = 8; p>0.99; H = 2.20), was significantly decreased compared to that of Mecp2f/y controls (464.7 ± 19.9 days; n = 38).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of survival data.

claim: The mean age of death in PV and VIP mutants was not significantly decreased compared to Mecp2f/y controls.
source: We found that the mean age of death in Mecp2–/y (71.5 ± 8.7 days; n = 13; p<0.00001; H = 57.06), Dlx5/6 mutants (118.5 ± 15.2 days; n = 10; p<0.00001; H = 45.63), and SST mutants (172.5 ± 12.2 days; n = 16; p<0.0001; H = 36.30), but not PV (493.5 ± 6.5 days; n = 18; p>0.99; H = −3.50) or VIP mutants (447.5 ± 52.5 days; n = 8; p>0.99; H = 2.20), was significantly decreased compared to that of Mecp2f/y controls (464.7 ± 19.9 days; n = 38).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of survival data.

claim: 100% of Mecp2–/y mice exhibited at least one seizure.
source: We found that 100% of Mecp2–/y (n = 10) and Dlx5/6 mutant (n = 13) mice exhibited at least one seizure
evidence: This is based on direct observation and counting of seizure incidence.

claim: 100% of Dlx5/6 mutant mice exhibited at least one seizure.
source: We found that 100% of Mecp2–/y (n = 10) and Dlx5/6 mutant (n = 13) mice exhibited at least one seizure
evidence: This is based on direct observation and counting of seizure incidence.

claim: 52.9% of SST mutants exhibited at least one seizure.
source: compared to only 52.9% of SST mutants (n = 36), 35.0% of PV mutants (n = 22), and 37.5% of VIP mutants (n = 8).
evidence: This is based on direct observation and counting of seizure incidence.

claim: 35.0% of PV mutants exhibited at least one seizure.
source: compared to only 52.9% of SST mutants (n = 36), 35.0% of PV mutants (n = 22), and 37.5% of VIP mutants (n = 8).
evidence: This is based on direct observation and counting of seizure incidence.

claim: 37.5% of VIP mutants exhibited at least one seizure.
source: compared to only 52.9% of SST mutants (n = 36), 35.0% of PV mutants (n = 22), and 37.5% of VIP mutants (n = 8).
evidence: This is based on direct observation and counting of seizure incidence.

claim: 17.1% of Mecp2f/y controls exhibited at least one seizure.
source: In comparison, the seizure rates in Mecp2f/y controls and in wild-types were 17.1% (n = 38) and 0% (n = 20), respectively
evidence: This is based on direct observation and counting of seizure incidence.

claim: 0% of wild-type mice exhibited seizures.
source: In comparison, the seizure rates in Mecp2f/y controls and in wild-types were 17.1% (n = 38) and 0% (n = 20), respectively
evidence: This is based on direct observation and counting of seizure incidence.

claim: The floxed allele contributes to the seizure phenotype.
source: In comparison, the seizure rates in Mecp2f/y controls and in wild-types were 17.1% (n = 38) and 0% (n = 20), respectively, suggesting a small contribution of the floxed allele to the seizure phenotype (Ito-Ishida et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in seizure rates between controls and wild-types, and is supported by a citation.

claim: The mean age of initial seizure was significantly earlier in Mecp2–/y mutants compared to Mecp2f/y controls.
source: The mean age of initial seizure was significantly earlier in Mecp2–/y mutants, but not the Dlx5/6, PV, SST, or VIP mutants, compared to Mecp2f/y controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of seizure onset ages shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The mean age of initial seizure was not significantly earlier in Dlx5/6, PV, SST, or VIP mutants compared to Mecp2f/y controls.
source: The mean age of initial seizure was significantly earlier in Mecp2–/y mutants, but not the Dlx5/6, PV, SST, or VIP mutants, compared to Mecp2f/y controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of seizure onset ages shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: MeCP2 depletion caused a modest change in LFP power in the 3–6 Hz range in the Dlx5/6 mutants.
source: MeCP2 depletion caused a modest change in LFP power, measured during periods of quiescence, in the 3–6 Hz range in the Dlx5/6 mutants (p=0.03; Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post-test), but not in other groups (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A robust broadband decrease in high-frequency LFP activity was observed in the Dlx5/6 mutants.
source: However, we observed a robust broadband decrease in high-frequency LFP activity in the Dlx5/6 mutants that was replicated in the VIP mutants, but not PV or SST mutants (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A robust broadband decrease in high-frequency LFP activity was observed in the VIP mutants.
source: However, we observed a robust broadband decrease in high-frequency LFP activity in the Dlx5/6 mutants that was replicated in the VIP mutants, but not PV or SST mutants (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There was a significant decrease in gamma-range (40–55 Hz) activity in Dlx5/6 mutants.
source: Quantification of high-frequency activity around the gamma (40–55 Hz) band revealed a significant decrease in gamma-range activity in both the Dlx5/6 (p=0.005) and VIP mutants (p=0.04; Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post-test; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on quantification of electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There was a significant decrease in gamma-range (40–55 Hz) activity in VIP mutants.
source: Quantification of high-frequency activity around the gamma (40–55 Hz) band revealed a significant decrease in gamma-range activity in both the Dlx5/6 (p=0.005) and VIP mutants (p=0.04; Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post-test; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on quantification of electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There was a loss of spike-field coherence in the gamma band in Dlx5/6 mutants.
source: We further found a loss of spike-field coherence in the gamma band in Dlx5/6 and VIP mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on spike-field coherence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a loss of spike-field coherence in the gamma band in VIP mutants.
source: We further found a loss of spike-field coherence in the gamma band in Dlx5/6 and VIP mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on spike-field coherence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hippocampal recordings revealed a loss of gamma-range LFP power in the Dlx5/6 mutants that was replicated by the SST mutants.
source: By contrast, hippocampal recordings revealed a loss of gamma-range LFP power in the Dlx5/6 mutants that was replicated by the SST mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is based on hippocampal electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of MeCP2 in the Dlx5/6 mutants led to a three-fold increase in the firing rates of regular-spiking, putative excitatory pyramidal neurons.
source: Single-unit recordings revealed that loss of MeCP2 in the Dlx5/6 mutants led to a three-fold increase in the firing rates of regular-spiking, putative excitatory pyramidal neurons as compared to that in control animals (p=0.004)
evidence: This is based on single-unit recordings and statistical analysis.

claim: The three-fold increase in firing rates observed in Dlx5/6 mutants was replicated in the VIP mutants.
source: Single-unit recordings revealed that loss of MeCP2 in the Dlx5/6 mutants led to a three-fold increase in the firing rates of regular-spiking, putative excitatory pyramidal neurons as compared to that in control animals (p=0.004), and this finding was replicated in the VIP (p=0.03) and SST (p=0.002; Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post-test) mutants (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on single-unit recordings and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The three-fold increase in firing rates observed in Dlx5/6 mutants was replicated in the SST mutants.
source: Single-unit recordings revealed that loss of MeCP2 in the Dlx5/6 mutants led to a three-fold increase in the firing rates of regular-spiking, putative excitatory pyramidal neurons as compared to that in control animals (p=0.004), and this finding was replicated in the VIP (p=0.03) and SST (p=0.002; Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post-test) mutants (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on single-unit recordings and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Cortical firing rates are robustly modulated by changes in behavioral state.
source: In previous work, we found that cortical firing rates are robustly modulated by changes in behavioral state, and are typically increased at the onset of locomotion (L) as compared to quiescence (Q) (Vinck et al., 2015).
evidence: This references previous work by the authors.

claim: Loss of normal VIP interneuron activity reduces state-dependent cortical modulation.
source: Loss of normal VIP interneuron activity reduces this state-dependent cortical modulation (Fu et al., 2014; Batista-Brito et al., 2017).
evidence: This references previous work by other groups.

claim: Pan-interneuron MeCP2 loss in the Dlx5/6 mutants led to decreased state-dependent modulation of single-unit cortical firing rates.
source: Both pan-interneuron MeCP2 loss in the Dlx5/6 mutants (p=0.004) and MeCP2 loss specific to VIP interneurons (p=0.02; Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post-test), but not other interneuron populations, led to decreased state-dependent modulation of single-unit cortical firing rates, measured as a modulation index [(FRL–FRQ)/(FRL+FRQ)] (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is based on analysis of state-dependent modulation shown in Figure 2F.

claim: MeCP2 loss specific to VIP interneurons led to decreased state-dependent modulation of single-unit cortical firing rates.
source: Both pan-interneuron MeCP2 loss in the Dlx5/6 mutants (p=0.004) and MeCP2 loss specific to VIP interneurons (p=0.02; Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post-test), but not other interneuron populations, led to decreased state-dependent modulation of single-unit cortical firing rates, measured as a modulation index [(FRL–FRQ)/(FRL+FRQ)] (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is based on analysis of state-dependent modulation shown in Figure 2F.

claim: MeCP2 loss from PV or SST interneurons did not lead to decreased state-dependent modulation of single-unit cortical firing rates.
source: Both pan-interneuron MeCP2 loss in the Dlx5/6 mutants (p=0.004) and MeCP2 loss specific to VIP interneurons (p=0.02; Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post-test), but not other interneuron populations, led to decreased state-dependent modulation of single-unit cortical firing rates, measured as a modulation index [(FRL–FRQ)/(FRL+FRQ)] (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is based on analysis of state-dependent modulation shown in Figure 2F.

claim: There were no differences in neural activity between Mecp2f/y controls, wild-types, and VipCre controls.
source: We did not find any differences in neural activity between Mecp2f/y controls, wild-types, and VipCre controls, suggesting that these results arise from cell type-specific Mecp2 loss of function (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on comparison of neural activity measures shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mecp2 mutations in GABAergic interneurons have been linked to key impairments in motor, repetitive, and social behaviors.
source: Previous work has linked Mecp2 mutations in GABAergic interneurons to key impairments in motor, repetitive, and social behaviors (Moretti et al., 2005; Chahrour and Zoghbi, 2007; Samaco et al., 2008; Chao et al., 2010; Kaufmann et al., 2012; He et al., 2014; Ito-Ishida et al., 2015).
evidence: This references multiple previous studies.

claim: No significant impairments in percentage of time spent in the open arms of the elevated plus maze task were found for the Dlx5/6, VIP, PV, or SST mutants compared to controls.
source: In agreement with previous work (Chao et al., 2010; Ito-Ishida et al., 2015), we found no significant impairments in percentage of time spent in the open arms of the elevated plus maze task, a measure of anxiety (Carobrez and Bertoglio, 2005), for the Dlx5/6, VIP, PV, or SST mutants compared to controls (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing shown in Figure 3A and references previous work.

claim: No impairment in locomotor behavior in the open field assay was found in any of the mutants.
source: Likewise, we found no impairment in locomotor behavior in the open field assay in any of the mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There was a significant impairment in marble burying in the pan-interneuron Dlx5/6 mutants compared to the controls.
source: By contrast, we found a significant impairment in marble burying, a measure of motor and repetitive behavior (Thomas et al., 2009; Silverman et al., 2010), in the pan-interneuron Dlx5/6 mutants compared to the controls (p=0.007).
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing and statistical analysis.

claim: The deficit in marble burying observed in the Dlx5/6 mutants was fully replicated in the VIP mutants.
source: The deficit observed in the Dlx5/6 mutants was fully replicated in the VIP mutants (p=0.001; Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post-test), but not in the PV or SST mutants (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The deficit in marble burying observed in the Dlx5/6 mutants was not replicated in the PV or SST mutants.
source: The deficit observed in the Dlx5/6 mutants was fully replicated in the VIP mutants (p=0.001; Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post-test), but not in the PV or SST mutants (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Control animals exhibited a significant preference for a chamber containing a conspecific over an empty chamber.
source: Control animals exhibited a significant preference for a chamber containing a conspecific over an empty chamber (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The pan-interneuron Dlx5/6 mutants exhibited a reverse preference for the empty chamber.
source: By contrast, the pan-interneuron Dlx5/6 mutants exhibited a reverse preference for the empty chamber (p=0.002).
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing and statistical analysis.

claim: The VIP mutants exhibited a reverse preference for the empty chamber over the conspecific.
source: The VIP mutants (p=0.002; Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post-test), but not the PV or SST mutants, fully replicated the effects of the pan-interneuron deletion, showing a significant preference for the empty chamber over the conspecific.
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing and statistical analysis.

claim: The PV and SST mutants did not exhibit a reverse preference for the empty chamber.
source: The VIP mutants (p=0.002; Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post-test), but not the PV or SST mutants, fully replicated the effects of the pan-interneuron deletion, showing a significant preference for the empty chamber over the conspecific.
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing and statistical analysis.

claim: Control animals made more approaches to the conspecific than to the empty holding cage.
source: In addition to altered overall social preferences, Mecp2 deletion affected the number of approaches mice made towards conspecifics. Control animals made more approaches to the conspecific than to the empty holding cage (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The Dlx5/6 mutants made more approaches to the empty holding cage than to the conspecific animal.
source: By contrast, the Dlx5/6 mutants made more approaches to the empty holding cage than to the conspecific animal (p=0.01).
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing and statistical analysis.

claim: The VIP mutants made more approaches to the empty holding cage than to the conspecific.
source: The VIP mutants (p=0.01; Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post-test), but not the PV or SST mutants, fully replicated these effects of pan-interneuron deletion, approaching the empty holding cage more than the conspecific.
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing and statistical analysis.

claim: The PV and SST mutants did not make more approaches to the empty holding cage than to the conspecific.
source: The VIP mutants (p=0.01; Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post-test), but not the PV or SST mutants, fully replicated these effects of pan-interneuron deletion, approaching the empty holding cage more than the conspecific.
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing and statistical analysis.

claim: VIP interneurons may contribute to the deficits in social behavior caused by global Mecp2 dysfunction.
source: Together, these data suggest that VIP interneurons may contribute to the deficits in social behavior caused by global Mecp2 dysfunction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data.

claim: There were no differences in behavior between Mecp2f/y controls, wild-types, and VipCre controls.
source: We did not find any differences in behavior between Mecp2f/y controls, wild-types, and VipCre controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting that these behavioral impairments arise as a consequence of cell-type-specific MeCP2 deletion.
evidence: This is based on behavioral testing shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mecp2 deletion from VIP interneurons recapitulates major phenotypes observed following pan-interneuron Mecp2 deletion at the levels of both neural activity and behavior.
source: We found that Mecp2 deletion from VIP interneurons recapitulates major phenotypes observed following pan-interneuron Mecp2 deletion at the levels of both neural activity and behavior (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Patients who have Rett Syndrome exhibit respiratory impairments and seizure.
source: Patients who have Rett Syndrome exhibit respiratory impairments and seizure (Chahrour and Zoghbi, 2007)
evidence: This references established clinical knowledge about Rett Syndrome.

claim: Respiratory impairments and seizure phenotypes are replicated in mouse models following deletion of Mecp2 from all GABAergic cells.
source: Patients who have Rett Syndrome exhibit respiratory impairments and seizure (Chahrour and Zoghbi, 2007), and these phenotypes are replicated in mouse models following deletion of Mecp2 from all GABAergic cells (Chao et al., 2010; Ito-Ishida et al., 2015).
evidence: This references previous mouse model studies.

claim: Mecp2 loss of function in SST interneurons conferred a late seizure phenotype.
source: In agreement with previous work (Ito-Ishida et al., 2015), we found that Mecp2 loss of function in SST interneurons conferred a late seizure phenotype.
evidence: This is based on seizure monitoring data and references previous work.

claim: Conditional mutations of Mecp2 in VIP interneurons did not increase seizure or mortality rates.
source: However, conditional mutations of Mecp2 in VIP interneurons did not increase seizure or mortality rates.
evidence: This is based on seizure and survival monitoring data.

claim: Mecp2 knockout animals had significantly earlier seizure onset and mortality than the Dlx5/6 mutants.
source: Mecp2 knockout animals had significantly earlier seizure onset and mortality than the Dlx5/6 mutants
evidence: This is based on comparison of seizure and survival data.

claim: Global loss of MeCP2 in excitatory neurons contributes to seizure.
source: Mecp2 knockout animals had significantly earlier seizure onset and mortality than the Dlx5/6 mutants, supporting previous findings that global loss of MeCP2 in excitatory neurons also contributes to seizure (Goffin et al., 2014; Meng et al., 2016)
evidence: This references previous findings about excitatory neuron contributions.

claim: Respiratory impairments in the Mecp2 knockouts may increase early mortality.
source: Mecp2 knockout animals had significantly earlier seizure onset and mortality than the Dlx5/6 mutants, supporting previous findings that global loss of MeCP2 in excitatory neurons also contributes to seizure (Goffin et al., 2014; Meng et al., 2016) and that respiratory impairments in the Mecp2 knockouts may increase early mortality (Chen et al., 2001; Guy et al., 2001).
evidence: This references previous findings about respiratory contributions to mortality.

claim: A previous study did not observe a seizure phenotype in Dlx5/6 mutants.
source: In comparison, a previous study did not observe a seizure phenotype in Dlx5/6 mutants, possibly as a result of methodological differences (Chao et al., 2010).
evidence: This references a previous study with different findings.

claim: A low rate of late-onset seizure was observed in the MeCP2f/y control animals.
source: We observed a low rate of late-onset seizure in the MeCP2f/y control animals
evidence: This is based on seizure monitoring data.

claim: The decrease in MeCP2 levels associated with the conditional allele may be associated with epileptogenic consequences.
source: We observed a low rate of late-onset seizure in the MeCP2f/y control animals, indicating that the decrease in MeCP2 levels associated with the conditional allele (Samaco et al., 2008) may be associated with epileptogenic consequences in addition to some mild behavioral phenotypes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the seizure data in control animals, referencing previous characterization of the conditional allele.

claim: Gamma-range activity is associated with cognition and sensory processing.
source: In particular, VIP mutants exhibited a decrease in cortical gamma-range activity, which is associated with cognition and sensory processing (Cardin, 2016; Cardin, 2018a)
evidence: This references established knowledge about gamma oscillations.

claim: Gamma-range activity may be impaired in Rett Syndrome.
source: In particular, VIP mutants exhibited a decrease in cortical gamma-range activity, which is associated with cognition and sensory processing (Cardin, 2016; Cardin, 2018a) and which may be impaired in Rett Syndrome (Peters et al., 2015).
evidence: This references previous work suggesting gamma impairments in Rett Syndrome.

claim: Loss of MeCP2 in the Dlx5/6 mutants caused a profound dysregulation of state-dependent modulation.
source: However, loss of MeCP2 in the VIP and Dlx5/6 mutants caused a profound dysregulation of this state-dependent modulation.
evidence: This is based on analysis of state-dependent modulation data.

claim: Loss of MeCP2 in the VIP mutants caused a profound dysregulation of state-dependent modulation.
source: However, loss of MeCP2 in the VIP and Dlx5/6 mutants caused a profound dysregulation of this state-dependent modulation.
evidence: This is based on analysis of state-dependent modulation data.

claim: The loss of modulation is unlikely to result from a 'ceiling effect' caused by increased overall firing rates.
source: This loss of modulation is unlikely to result from a 'ceiling effect' caused by increased overall firing rates, as putative excitatory neurons in the SST and VIP mutants exhibited equally enhanced firing but only the VIP mutants showed a loss of state-dependent modulation.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the data comparing SST and VIP mutants.

claim: VIP interneurons are thought to play a key role in regulating the state-dependent modulation of cortical circuits.
source: VIP interneurons are thought to play a key role in regulating the state-dependent modulation of cortical circuits, partly via strong inhibition of SST interneurons and consequent disinhibition of pyramidal neurons (Pi et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2014; Prönneke et al., 2015; Karnani et al., 2016; Muñoz et al., 2017).
evidence: This references multiple previous studies about VIP interneuron function.

claim: Developmental perturbation of VIP interneurons by conditional deletion of ErbB4 caused a loss of state-dependent cortical regulation.
source: We had previously found that developmental perturbation of VIP interneurons by conditional deletion of the schizophrenia-associated gene ErbB4 caused a similar loss of state-dependent cortical regulation (Batista-Brito et al., 2017).
evidence: This references previous work by the authors.

claim: Disruption of state-dependent cortical dynamics may be a common outcome of disease mechanisms affecting VIP interneurons.
source: Together, these findings suggest that disruption of state-dependent cortical dynamics may be a common outcome of disease mechanisms affecting VIP interneurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation combining current and previous findings.

claim: Previous work has highlighted alterations in repetitive and motor behaviors, but not anxiety, following GABAergic deletion of Mecp2.
source: Previous work has highlighted alterations in repetitive and motor behaviors, but not anxiety, following GABAergic deletion of Mecp2 (Chao et al., 2010; Ito-Ishida et al., 2015; Ure et al., 2016).
evidence: This references previous behavioral studies.

claim: Marble burying is a task that is susceptible to altered anxiety and OCD-like behaviors as well as changes in fine motor function.
source: However, the pan-interneuron Dlx5/6 mutants exhibited deficits in marble burying, a task that is susceptible to altered anxiety and OCD-like behaviors as well as changes in fine motor function (Thomas et al., 2009; Silverman et al., 2010).
evidence: This references previous characterization of the marble burying task.

claim: Abnormal or reduced social behavior is a hallmark of many autism spectrum disorder models.
source: Abnormal or reduced social behavior is a hallmark of many autism spectrum disorder models, and has previously been shown in mice lacking MeCP2 in all GABAergic populations (Chao et al., 2010; Ito-Ishida et al., 2015).
evidence: This references established knowledge about autism models and previous Mecp2 studies.

claim: SST-specific deletion led to loss of any social preference.
source: Notably, Mecp2 deletion from VIP, but not from PV or SST, interneurons fully replicated this phenotype. SST-specific deletion led to loss of any social preference, suggesting a potential contribution of both VIP- and SST-expressing cells to deficits in social behavior following global Mecp2 loss of function.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data showing SST mutants had no preference.

claim: Both VIP- and SST-expressing cells may contribute to deficits in social behavior following global Mecp2 loss of function.
source: SST-specific deletion led to loss of any social preference, suggesting a potential contribution of both VIP- and SST-expressing cells to deficits in social behavior following global Mecp2 loss of function.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the social behavior data.

claim: The behavioral findings in the Dlx5/6, PV and SST mutants are in general agreement with previous work.
source: Overall, our behavioral findings in the Dlx5/6, PV and SST mutants are in general agreement with previous work (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature.

claim: The PvalbCre line used in this study largely expresses Cre recombinase in PV interneurons, along with some thalamocortical projection neurons.
source: The PvalbCre line used here largely expresses Cre recombinase in PV interneurons, along with some thalamocortical projection neurons (Hippenmeyer et al., 2005; Cardin et al., 2009).
evidence: This references previous characterization of the Cre line.

claim: The Pvalb-2A-Cre line also expresses Cre in a subset of cortical pyramidal neurons and additional thalamic nuclei.
source: In comparison, the Pvalb-2A-Cre line used in some previous work (Goffin et al., 2014; Ito-Ishida et al., 2015) also expresses Cre in a subset of cortical pyramidal neurons and additional thalamic nuclei (Madisen et al., 2010).
evidence: This references previous characterization of a different Cre line.
